newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn to cut solidarity tax two points in '98 - Bild.
newsitem.headline: Bonn to cut solidarity tax two points in '98 - Bild.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats have agreed to a demand from their coalition partners to cut the unpopular solidarity tax two percentage points to 5.5 percent in 1998, the Bild newspaper reported on Monday.

The tax, aimed at helping to finance the reconstruction of formerly communist east Germany, was to have been cut one point in January 1997 and a further point in 1998, but that plan was recently scrapped to fill a 1997 budget gap.

Kohl's junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP) lobbied hard for a fresh pledge to cut the tax, and convinced their coalition partners at a weekend meeting of a government tax reform commission headed by Finance Minister Theo Waigel, Bild said.
No other taxes will be increased in compensation, it said.
Bild quoted Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt as saying: "We are on the way to a solution the FDP wants."
Juergen Moellemann, head of the FDP in North Rhine-Westphalia, told Bild: "After talks with coalition leaders I am sure that the solidarity tax will be cut two percentage points on January 1, 1998."
